answer.rationale: Primary objective is minimizing total cost of ownership without increasing delivery risk. Memory_c2 indicates that a prior switch to the low-cost vendor yielded sharp unit-cost savings with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing, which directly supports the viability of switching. Memory_c1 shows that renewing with the incumbent preserved integration stability across two cycles with no migration disruption, which is the key delivery-risk counterargument I need to weigh. The incumbent has refused to reopen price, so negotiate_terms is not viable this cycle. The low-cost vendor's quote meets the 18% finance mandate alone, which no other option achieves. Memory_c3 confirms that adding a second source is a valuable risk mitigation but is the second-priority decision; with only one action slot this cycle, the cost mandate takes precedence, and the prior evidence suggests the low-cost vendor's onboarding was quick enough to complete within the 14-day window. Memory_c6 (multi-year volume pricing with the incumbent) is moot given their refusal to renegotiate. The assembly line at 94% with no buffer is the primary delivery risk, but memory_c2's record of accurate invoicing and quick onboarding reduces confidence that the switch itself will disrupt deliveries. If memory_c2 surfaces material integration risk not captured in the summary, I will fall back to renew_incumbent on month-to-month terms (as done in memory_c5) and push the cost-mandate conversation to next cycle.
